part_title: Model Monitor, Clarify and Production Drift

scenes.title: Monitor Drift and Act
scenes.narration: This slide describes the loop for existing SageMaker Model Monitor users. First, create a baseline from representative training data and capture statistics and constraints. Second, enable data capture from an endpoint so inference inputs and predictions can be analysed. Third, compare current records against baseline behavior. Fourth, send monitoring metrics or violations to CloudWatch, where alarms can notify the team. Finally, investigate whether the change reflects bad input quality, a genuine shift in the population, or something requiring retraining. The arrow returns to the baseline and model because monitoring leads to action, not just dashboards. Notice the slide's existing-customer qualification. Product availability and onboarding restrictions must be checked before planning new use. Also remember that drift detection alone doesn't prove the model's predictions have become inaccurate; pair it with ground truth and business metrics wherever possible.

scenes.title: Explain Predictions and Inspect Bias
scenes.narration: Amazon SageMaker Clarify is illustrated as a tool for explaining predictions and examining potential bias in model data or outputs. Follow the left path: a training dataset and a trained model enter the analysis workflow. The central panels separate pre-training bias analysis, post-training prediction disparities, and feature attribution. Those are different questions. A dataset can have uneven representation before a model is trained, while a deployed model can produce different outcomes across groups even when data representation seems balanced. Attribution methods such as SHAP attempt to identify which features influence an individual prediction or aggregate behavior. On the right, human experts interpret the resulting charts and decide whether mitigation is required. The slide identifies existing-customer restrictions for the depicted capability. Metrics are indicators requiring contextual review, not automatic legal or ethical judgments.

scenes.title: Bias Metrics Need Context
scenes.narration: This slide presents four bias-related measurements. Class imbalance compares sizes of demographic groups in the available data. Difference in positive label proportions checks whether favorable labels occur at different rates. Distribution divergence measures how differently outcome distributions appear across groups. Conditional demographic disparity introduces a relevant conditioning attribute so comparisons reflect a chosen context. Notice the caution at the bottom: none of these numbers automatically declares that a model is fair or unfair. Data quality, task definition, sample size and legitimate conditioning variables matter. A single low metric can conceal harms elsewhere; a high metric may require investigation rather than immediate rejection. Responsible evaluation compares multiple metrics and documents why particular attributes, labels and thresholds were selected. The core learning point is to use bias measurements as evidence for investigation and mitigation, not as self-executing approval gates.

scenes.title: Schedule a Monitoring Loop
scenes.narration: This flow shows a scheduled monitoring process. The first panel stores baseline statistics and constraints in S3. The next enables endpoint data capture to collect representative inference inputs and predictions. A scheduled SageMaker Model Monitor analysis then examines captured data against the baseline. Findings flow to CloudWatch metrics and alarms. Finally, a remediation process investigates, updates data or model logic and may initiate retraining. Trace the orange return line labeled continuous monitoring. Baselines should be reconsidered when the approved data definition changes, not blindly replaced whenever an alert appears. The results only mean something if the captured requests are representative and sensitive content is protected. This slide concerns functionality for existing supported Model Monitor users, so verify current service eligibility before adopting it in a new environment.

scenes.title: Four Monitoring Questions
scenes.narration: The slide organizes monitoring around four questions. First, data quality: do production features resemble the approved training baseline in schema and statistical distribution? Second, model quality: do recent predictions agree with actual outcomes once those labels are available? Third, bias drift: are predictions becoming systematically less equitable across relevant groups? Fourth, feature-attribution drift: has the model begun depending on different input features than before? Look at each baseline-versus-production miniature chart. A change in input distribution is not necessarily a performance failure, and model quality cannot always be measured without delayed ground-truth labels. The bottom message is to choose the checks that are meaningful for a particular deployment and investigate together. A monitoring dashboard is a diagnostic tool, not an automatic retraining justification. Production governance must distinguish a genuine regression from harmless seasonal change.
